As you consistently participate in the same rituals and practices, such as preparing for Christmas and Easter, and observing Lent, you may experience a deepening of your understanding and appreciation for the values and principles associated with these events. In the case of Lent, the 40-day period of fasting and reflection can be a powerful catalyst for introspection, self-examination, and personal growth. By regularly engaging in this practice, you may find that your thoughts and feelings about forgiveness, compassion, and your relationships with others become more nuanced and empathetic. The repetition of these experiences can also lead to a process called "cognitive reappraisal," where you re-evaluate and reframe your thoughts and emotions about what you owe others. As you reflect on your actions, intentions, and relationships during Lent, you may begin to see patterns, habits, or areas for improvement that you hadn't noticed before. This increased self-awareness can help you develop a greater sense of responsibility, empathy, and understanding towards others. Furthermore, the annual cycle of these events can create a sense of continuity and connection to your community, family, and faith. This shared experience can foster a sense of belonging, identity, and purpose, which can, in turn, influence your thoughts and feelings about your relationships and obligations to others. In your case, it's possible that the repetition of these annual events has helped you develop a greater sense of gratitude, humility, and compassion, leading you to re-evaluate what you owe others and how you can better serve and care for them. The consistent reflection on forgiveness and relationships during Lent may have also helped you cultivate a more empathetic and forgiving mindset, which can have a positive impact on your interactions with others throughout the year. Overall, the repetition of meaningful experiences like Christmas, Easter, and Lent can indeed shape your thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, leading to a deeper understanding of what you owe others and how you can nurture more positive, compassionate relationships.

Scenario:
AITA for asking my boyfriend to pick up and drop off my child on weekends which made him suggest a break up? | So for full disclosure my partner works full time and is usually at work from 7am-7pm, and I have a weekend job that requires me to be away from 9am-12pm. We don’t live together but we are local so we are always in and out of each other’s homes. My son decided he wanted to play football on weekends- he’s 12 years old and really excited about it. I was initially going to ask my bf if he could pay for it but I mentioned it to my mum when I went around for a cup of tea and she was strongly expecting me to pay and told me it was my responsibility not my bf’s... even though he’s been in my life 3 years. So I ended up having to pay but in order to afford it I extended my hours at work to 9-5. I asked my bf if he’d be willing to pick up and drop off my son on weekends as obviously if be at work and he looked uncomfortable and said sorry no can’t his dad drop him? I admit I snapped at him and told him that his dad lives in south London whereas we live in north London and his dad doesn’t drive but my boyfriend does. I asked him if he really wanted to be part of this family and if he did he wouldn’t mind doing small stuff like this for me. I suppose his dad COULD take him but what would be a 1 hour + journey for his dad would take 15 minutes for my bf. He got really angry and told me that he was having to work longer hours to support me and my son and that he wanted to use his weekends to go to football games etc as I wasn’t at home anyway. He said that he wanted to chill and relax and that I was forcing things on him way too quick. He then suggested that we break up bc ”I was putting too many responsibilities on him” and I was like.. really? Over a bloody football game? Welcome to the real world love! The little sneak then went over to see my mum and had a heart to heart with her which ended up in HER calling ME and her telling me I am out of line. Who is TA? AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw:
I would say: 1 (You are the asshole).

While it's understandable that you need help with picking up and dropping off your son, it seems like you approached the situation with a sense of entitlement and expectation that your boyfriend would automatically agree to take on this responsibility. You also snapped at him when he expressed his discomfort, which is not a constructive way to communicate.

Additionally, it's clear that your boyfriend feels like he's already contributing to your life and your son's life in significant ways, including working long hours to support you both. He may feel like he needs some downtime on the weekends to recharge, and it's reasonable that he wouldn't want to take on additional responsibilities without being asked or discussed beforehand.

It's also worth noting that your boyfriend's suggestion to break up may not be just about the football game, but about the larger dynamic of your relationship and how you communicate with each other. It's possible that he feels like you're not considering his needs or boundaries, and that you're putting too much pressure on him to take on responsibilities without discussing them first.

Your reaction to his suggestion to break up, dismissing his concerns and telling him to "welcome to the real world," comes across as dismissive and unempathetic. It's possible that you could have handled the situation with more understanding and communication, rather than getting defensive and angry.

Overall, while it's understandable that you need help with childcare, it's clear that there are deeper issues in your relationship that need to be addressed, and it's not just about the football game.
